children: Kratos Defense & Security Solutions
and GE Aerospace
said Monday they successfully completed an ignition test of their GEK800 turbofan engine, advancing a propulsion program aimed at cruise missiles and other unmanned military systems.
The first serial-numbered GEK800 engine was tested at Kratos’ X-58 facility and successfully ignited, starting a new phase of testing. The companies said the program remains on schedule.
The GEK800, which has received the military designation F143-ZZ-100, is an 800-pound-thrust turbofan designed for long-range missiles and other unmanned applications.
Commercial significance
For investors, the test is notable because the GEK800 has moved beyond an internally funded technology demonstration.
Kratos
and GE Aerospace

said in August that the U.S. Air Force awarded an engineering, manufacturing and development contract for the F143 as a second-source propulsion system for the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, or JASSM. The companies didn't disclose the value of that contract.
That makes Monday's ignition test another development milestone toward potential production rather than an indication of new revenue by itself.
Kratos
is preparing for potential large-volume production of the engine. The company hasn't disclosed expected production volumes, pricing or the timing of possible production orders.
Engine passed earlier tests
The GEK800 has been undergoing development and testing for several years. Kratos
and GE Aerospace
began working together on the program in 2023 with support from the Air Force Research Laboratory.

The companies had completed more than 50 ground-test engine starts by August. The GEK800 also completed altitude testing at Purdue University's Zucrow Laboratories in 2025, including durability and engine-limits testing.
GE Aerospace

said earlier this year that the first GEK800 was designed, built and tested in less than 12 months. The company has described small military engines as a growth area as demand increases for cruise missiles and unmanned aircraft.
Investors await production orders
The investment implications are potentially more significant for Kratos
than GE Aerospace
because of the companies' relative size.

Kratos has been investing in propulsion systems for missiles, drones and other unmanned platforms as part of its strategy to produce relatively low-cost military systems in larger quantities. GE Aerospace, by comparison, operates a much larger commercial and military engine business.

The next milestones will therefore matter more than Monday's ignition alone. Investors will be watching the F143's progress through engineering and development, integration with JASSM and whether the program ultimately leads to meaningful production orders.

GE Aerospace has also been expanding the concept into a family of smaller military engines. Its GEK1500 program, also being developed with Kratos, is aimed at applications including unmanned aircraft, collaborative combat aircraft and missiles.

The successful GEK800 test reduces some technical development risk, but it doesn't establish the eventual size or profitability of the program. Those questions will depend largely on procurement decisions, production volumes and Kratos' economics if the engine advances into large-scale manufacturing.

title: Kratos, GE Aerospace advance cruise missile engine with ignition test
